scan.summary: This is Cascade Specialty Chemicals' written emergency action plan for the Portland facility, required under OSHA 1910.38 and Oregon OSHA 437-002-0042. It describes what the facility's 42 employees—warehouse, drivers, laboratory, and office staff—must do during fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake or other emergencies. The document covers evacuation procedures, assembly point location, accounting for all personnel after evacuation, alarm signals, shelter-in-place procedures, rescue and medical response, and annual training and review cycles.
scan.freshness_note: This plan was last revised February 2021, nearly five years ago as of September 2026. OSHA requires review and update annually under 1910.38(e). Because this was revised in 2021 and there has been no documented update in over four years, you should ask whether the plan has been reviewed and updated annually per the stated requirement in section 6, and whether the appendices (evacuation maps and rosters) are current.

gaps.title: No accountability for contractors and visitors
gaps.description: The scope in section 1 states the plan applies to contractors and visitors while on-site, but the evacuation procedures do not explain how contractors and visitors—who may not be on the daily sign-in sheet or visitor log—are accounted for after evacuation. OSHA 1910.38(a)(4) requires procedures to account for all employees after evacuation. While contractors and visitors are in scope, there is no documented method to identify who is present or how their absence would be detected.
gaps.fix: Add a specific procedure for how contractors and visitors are tracked before and after evacuation (e.g., sign-in/out log, escort responsibility, or sweep-team responsibility). Designate who is responsible for collecting and verifying contractor/visitor information at the assembly point.
gaps.locator: Section 1 (scope); Section 4 (accounting for employees after evacuation)
gaps.quote: It applies to all 42 employees at the Portland facility, including warehouse, drivers, laboratory and office staff, and to contractors and visitors while on site.

gaps.title: No plan for facility restart after emergency
gaps.description: The plan does not include procedures for assessing whether the facility is safe to re-occupy, restoring normal operations, or resuming business activities after an emergency. Section 3 states employees do not re-enter until the fire department or incident coordinator gives the all-clear, but there are no procedures for post-emergency assessment, damage evaluation, or controlled facility restart.
gaps.fix: Add a section on post-emergency procedures covering: (1) who conducts facility safety assessment; (2) criteria for determining building re-occupancy is safe; (3) procedures for restoring utilities, ventilation, and other critical systems; (4) incident documentation and reporting requirements; (5) notification to employees of restart or continued closure.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38(a) general requirement for a complete plan; emergency management best practices

gaps.title: No emergency contact information or communication protocol
gaps.description: The plan does not identify an emergency coordinator or incident coordinator by name or contact information, nor does it detail how that person communicates with fire department, medical services, or regulatory agencies. Section 4 mentions "the incident coordinator at the assembly point," but this person is not named, and there is no procedure for how that individual is notified of an emergency or how they communicate information outside the facility. Section 6 requires the plan to include names or job titles of employees to contact for more information, but the warden roster (Appendix B) is not provided.
gaps.fix: Add the name, title, and 24-hour contact information of the incident coordinator (primary and backup). Add procedures for communication with external agencies (fire department, EMS, regulatory agencies). Ensure Appendix B (floor warden and first-aid responder roster) is completed and attached, with names and contact information visible.
gaps.locator: Section 1 (required in scope); Section 4 (incident coordinator role); Section 6 (required by standard)
gaps.quote: who passes the information to the fire department on arrival

gaps.title: No environmental or regulatory notification procedures
gaps.description: Cascade Specialty Chemicals is a chemical distributor. A chemical release may trigger reporting obligations under CERCLA Section 103 (reportable quantities), Oregon Revised Statutes (hazardous waste rules), EPA RMP (Risk Management Program) if applicable, or state environmental agency notification. The plan does not specify what constitutes a reportable release, who notifies regulatory agencies, what information is provided, or when notification occurs.
gaps.fix: Add a section on regulatory reporting: (1) identify which chemicals in inventory are CERCLA reportable or have reportable quantities; (2) define at what point a release requires notification to Oregon DEQ, EPA, or other agencies; (3) name the responsible person for making those notifications; (4) include contact information and reporting templates; (5) document the regulatory timeline (e.g., immediate, 24 hours, etc.); (6) identify what constitutes a release (visible spill, vapor plume, soil contamination, etc.).
gaps.citation: CERCLA Section 103 (42 USC 9603); Oregon DEQ rules on hazardous waste and spill reporting; OSHA 1910.38(a) and 1910.1200 (Hazard Communication)

Verify: (1) maps show exit routes, assembly point, shelter-in-place locations, emergency shower/eyewash location; (2) rosters list names, titles, and current contact information for each floor warden (one per area) and first-aid responder (two per shift); (3) maps are up to date and match current building layout; (4) rosters reflect current staffing.
gaps.citation: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.38(a) requires written plan with all procedures; 1910.38(c)(6) requires names or job titles of designated personnel; best practice includes posted evacuation maps

gaps.title: Assembly point distance specified but not verified as safe
gaps.description: Section 3 specifies the assembly point as "the far north end of the visitor parking lot, beside the flagpole, at least 150 feet from the building." The distance of 150 feet is specified, but there is no documentation that this location has been verified as safe from secondary hazards (e.g., chemical vapor, falling debris, downwind of release location, proximity to roads with traffic). OSHA 1910.38(a)(2) requires adequate assembly points. NFPA 101 Life Safety Code and EPA shelter-in-place guidance recommend consideration of wind direction, ground contamination, and structural stability.
gaps.fix: Add documentation of assembly point safety assessment: (1) conduct a site assessment of the visitor parking lot and flagpole location for hazards (terrain, weather exposure, proximity to facility, wind patterns); (2) verify that 150 feet is adequate for all credible emergency scenarios (fire, chemical release, earthquake); (3) identify alternative assembly points if primary location is unsafe during specific scenarios (e.g., west wind carries chemical vapor to north end); (4) document the assessment, findings, and sign-off by facilities lead; (5) review annually or when building/surrounding area changes.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38(a)(2) requires adequate assembly points; NFPA 101 Life Safety Code Section 4.7.8; EPA guidance on shelter-in-place
gaps.quote: The assembly point is the far north end of the visitor parking lot, beside the flagpole, at least 150 feet from the building.

gaps.title: No evidence of training completion
gaps.description: Section 6 describes training requirements (new employee orientation, annual training for floor wardens and first-aid responders, review upon plan changes), but there is no mention of training records, sign-in sheets, competency verification, or documentation. OSHA 1910.38(a) and (e) require training, and Oregon OSHA expects documentation of who received training, when, and the content.
gaps.fix: Establish a training documentation system: (1) maintain a sign-in sheet for each training session (date, attendees, topics covered, trainer name); (2) create a training matrix tracking which employees have completed initial orientation, indicating date; (3) track floor warden and first-aid responder annual training dates and expiration of certifications; (4) document that new hires are trained on day one (initial orientation record); (5) file training records centrally and review annually as part of plan review.
gaps.citation: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.38(a) and (e) require training; Oregon OSHA 437-002-0042(5) requires review with employees; standard practice requires documentation
gaps.quote: Every new employee is walked through this plan

gaps.title: No record of evacuation drills
gaps.description: Section 4 states that "evacuation drills are held twice a year, in spring and autumn," but there is no documentation requirement, no drill records, no scenario descriptions, no observation/findings, or no corrective actions. OSHA 1910.38 and Oregon OSHA expect documentation of drills, participant list, timing, any issues observed, and corrective actions taken.
gaps.fix: Create and maintain an evacuation drill log: (1) for each drill, record the date, time, announced or unannounced, scenario (fire, chemical release, shelter-in-place, etc.), number of participants, duration, any personnel unable to participate and why, issues observed (exit blocked, slow reporting to assembly point, etc.), corrective actions identified, and responsible party for follow-up; (2) file the log annually; (3) review drill results in the annual plan review; (4) after drills, brief all employees on findings and lessons learned.
gaps.citation: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.38(a); Oregon OSHA 437-002-0042; NFPA 101 and emergency management best practices
gaps.quote: Evacuation drills are held twice a year, in spring and autumn.

gaps.title: No hazmat-specific response procedures
gaps.description: Cascade Specialty Chemicals is a chemical distributor, yet the plan does not identify which chemicals are stored or distributed, their hazards, or specific response procedures beyond directing an exposed employee to the emergency shower. There are no procedures for containment of spills, initial response to vapor release, coordination with Hazmat teams, isolation of a contaminated area, or use of personal protective equipment during response. OSHA 1910.1200 (Hazard Communication) requires knowledge of chemical hazards; 1910.1450 and emergency response standards expect specific procedures.
gaps.fix: Add a hazmat-specific section: (1) create or attach a chemical inventory identifying high-hazard chemicals and their locations (warehouse, loading dock, lab); (2) for each chemical or chemical class (e.g., organic solvents, corrosives, oxidizers), specify: emergency response procedures, personal protective equipment required, evacuation or shelter-in-place decision criteria, spill containment steps, maximum safe duration of exposure, and medical attention needed; (3) reference SDS (Safety Data Sheet) locations and require that SDSs be available at the assembly point; (4) identify when to request hazmat response (fire department hazmat team or environmental response contractor); (5) describe initial response by facility personnel before hazmat arrives (e.g., 'isolate area, do not enter vapors, ensure ventilation').
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.1200 (Hazard Communication); 1910.1450 (Occupational Exposure to Hazardous Chemicals in Labs); CERCLA Section 103 for reportable quantities; OSHA 1910.38(a)(1) requires identification of workplace hazards
gaps.locator: Not in the document; chemical inventory and hazmat response missing from all sections

gaps.title: No post-emergency procedures or incident reporting
gaps.description: The plan ends at evacuation and initial first aid. There are no procedures for what happens after an incident is resolved: incident documentation, injury reporting, root cause analysis, corrective actions, regulatory reporting, or communication with affected employees. OSHA 1910.38(a) implies a complete emergency management cycle; OSHA 1904 requires injury recordkeeping if an injury occurs.
gaps.fix: Add a section on post-emergency and incident management: (1) incident documentation—who completes the incident report, what information is captured (date, time, cause, personnel involved, injuries, damage, regulatory notifications); (2) injury reporting and OSHA 1904 recordkeeping compliance; (3) root cause analysis process; (4) corrective action tracking; (5) communication with affected employees and regulatory agencies; (6) document retention and archival; (7) lessons learned review in the annual plan review cycle.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38(a) and general occupational safety best practices; OSHA 1904 (Recording and Reporting Occupational Injuries and Illnesses)

gaps.title: No procedure for persons with disabilities or access limitations
gaps.description: The plan does not address employees with disabilities, mobility limitations, hearing impairment, visual impairment, or other conditions that might affect evacuation or emergency response. ADA Title I requires equal access accommodations. The plan describes standard evacuation (stop work, leave by nearest exit, go to assembly point) without considering whether all employees can execute these steps.
gaps.fix: Add a section on accommodations for employees with disabilities: (1) during initial hiring and onboarding, identify any employees with mobility, hearing, visual, or other impairments that affect emergency response; (2) for each identified employee, develop an individual emergency action plan specifying: their evacuation method or assisted evacuation, assignment of a buddy/escort, alternative assembly point if accessible, specific training needs, communication method (visual alerts for deaf employees, audible alerts for blind employees), and any special equipment (mobility aid, medical device, etc.); (3) brief the assigned buddy/floor warden on the accommodation plan; (4) document the plan and review annually or upon status change.
gaps.citation: ADA Title I (employer obligation to provide equal access); OSHA 1910.38(a) best practices; NFPA guidance on emergency procedures for persons with disabilities

gaps.title: No external communication or media procedures
gaps.description: If an incident is serious (injury, large chemical release, environmental contamination), it may attract media attention or trigger regulatory inquiries. The plan does not specify who speaks to media, what information is released, how employee family members are informed, or how external communication is managed. OSHA 1910.38(a)(4) requires procedures for reporting emergencies, which extends to external stakeholders.
gaps.fix: Add a section on external communication: (1) designate a single point of contact for external inquiries (media, regulatory agencies, customer calls); (2) establish communication chain (e.g., incident coordinator notifies management, management approves media statement); (3) define what information may be released to media (confirmed facts only, no speculation); (4) if an employee is injured, establish a process to notify next-of-kin; (5) draft template statements for different scenarios (fire with no injuries, chemical release requiring evacuation, injury requiring medical transport); (6) identify when legal counsel or company management must approve statements.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38(a)(4) procedures for reporting emergencies; emergency management best practices; legal and public relations consideration

gaps.title: Plan distribution and access unclear
gaps.description: Section 1 states the plan "is kept in the front office and in the warehouse break room, and a copy is available to any employee on request." However, there is no specification of whether all employees receive a copy, whether copies are posted in other areas, or how employees know where to access it. The plan may be difficult to access in an actual emergency if located only in two rooms.
gaps.fix: Clarify plan distribution and access: (1) specify that the plan is available in physical and/or electronic form; (2) identify locations where printed copies are posted (front office, warehouse break room, laboratory); (3) state that all new employees receive a copy or link at hire; (4) if electronic, specify how to access (shared drive, intranet, printed on request); (5) note that evacuation maps (Appendix A) must be posted at each exit door and in work areas per OSHA 1910.35; (6) ensure copies are accessible during an emergency (not locked in a cabinet).
gaps.citation: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.38(b) requires plan be available to employees for review; 1910.35 requires exit route signs and maps
gaps.quote: The plan is kept in the front office and in the warehouse break room, and a copy is available to any employee on request.

gaps.title: Shelter-in-place procedures incomplete
gaps.description: Section 3 describes the shelter-in-place signal (three short horns) and actions (move to interior conference room or laboratory corridor, close doors, facilities lead shuts down ventilation). However, the procedure lacks detail: how long are employees expected to remain sheltered, what is the signal or trigger to resume normal operations, how is ventilation restarted, are there supplies (water, first aid) in the shelter area, are there communication systems to alert sheltered personnel, and how are persons who were outside the building during shelter-in-place notified to avoid returning?
gaps.fix: Expand the shelter-in-place section with: (1) specific location names and capacities (e.g., 'interior conference room on the second floor, max 20 persons'); (2) procedures for who may enter the shelter area and in what order; (3) ventilation shutdown procedure and who is responsible; (4) communication method to inform sheltered personnel of situation and expected duration; (5) supplies maintained in shelter area (drinking water, first-aid kit, blankets for injured); (6) all-clear signal or procedure to exit shelter (when and how is it safe to leave); (7) procedure to prevent persons outside from re-entering during shelter-in-place (e.g., guard at entry, public announcement); (8) time estimate for typical shelter-in-place duration (e.g., 'until outdoor hazard disperses, typically 1-4 hours').
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38(a) requires procedures for all emergencies; EPA/FEMA shelter-in-place guidance (www.ready.gov); NFPA 1600
gaps.quote: Employees move to the interior conference room or the laboratory corridor, close doors, and the facilities lead shuts down the building ventilation from the mechanical room panel.

gaps.title: No mutual aid or resource-sharing agreement
gaps.description: The plan does not mention mutual aid arrangements with neighboring facilities or vendors, shared resources (e.g., equipment rental, temporary shelter, first-aid supplies), or how to request assistance from city emergency services for specialized response (hazmat, heavy rescue, medical mass care). In a significant incident, Cascade may need external resources beyond its own staff and equipment.
gaps.fix: Add a section on resource and mutual aid: (1) identify critical resources needed in emergencies (medical supplies, temporary shelter for uninjured employees, decontamination equipment, hazmat response); (2) identify mutual aid partners (neighboring chemical companies, local fire department hazmat team, medical providers, environmental cleanup contractors); (3) establish or reference mutual aid agreements (if formal agreements exist, attach a copy); (4) provide contact information for resource providers; (5) specify the incident coordinator's authority to request external assistance.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38(a) and emergency management best practices; no specific OSHA mandate but standard practice for chemical facilities

gaps.title: No information on hazard identification and chemical inventory
gaps.description: As a chemical distributor, Cascade's emergency preparedness must be based on identification of hazards present. The plan does not reference a chemical inventory, hazard assessment, or list of chemicals stored at the facility. This is foundational information needed to design appropriate procedures, training, and response actions.
gaps.fix: Create and attach a chemical inventory: (1) list all chemicals stored, distributed, or handled at the Portland facility, including location (warehouse, loading dock, lab), quantity, and primary hazards (flammable, corrosive, reactive, toxic, health hazard); (2) identify chemicals with reportable quantities under CERCLA or other regulations; (3) attach or reference SDS for each chemical; (4) identify areas of highest concern (e.g., solvent storage, corrosive cabinet); (5) note any process hazards (mixing, heating, pressure) that could increase emergency risk; (6) review the inventory annually and update if products, quantities, or locations change.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.1200 (Hazard Communication) requires knowledge of chemical hazards; 1910.38(a)(1) requires identification of workplace hazards; EPA RMP regulations for high-hazard chemicals

gaps.title: Missing reference to related plans or policies
gaps.description: The emergency action plan exists in a vacuum—there is no reference to or coordination with other required or recommended plans: fire prevention plan (OSHA 1910.39), security/active threat procedures, medical emergency response procedures, business continuity plan, or environmental spill response procedures. A chemical facility should integrate these into a cohesive emergency management system.
gaps.fix: Add a section on related plans and integration: (1) reference the facility's fire prevention plan (OSHA 1910.39) and describe how emergency action plan procedures support it; (2) identify other plans in place (security, medical, environmental response, business continuity); (3) note where copies are kept and who maintains them; (4) describe how these plans interact (e.g., if a fire ignites a chemical spill, both the fire evacuation and hazmat response procedures apply); (5) designate a single person responsible for coordinating all emergency-related documents; (6) include a cross-reference table in an appendix.
gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.38 and 1910.39 (fire prevention plan); emergency management best practices; integration of EAP with other plans

Chemical inventory and specific hazard information are completely absent, making it impossible to judge whether procedures are adequate for the chemicals actually present. The identification of 'incident coordinator' as a role is clear, but no actual person is named, and no backup is designated. First-aid responder certifications are not mentioned—unclear if they hold current CPR/First Aid credentials. Shelter-in-place procedure is outlined at high level but lacks operational details on capacity, duration, supplies, and all-clear criteria. Overall, the document establishes a basic emergency action structure but lacks the documentation, detail, and supporting appendices needed for confident assessment of adequacy.

CASCADE SPECIALTY CHEMICALS, LLC
EMERGENCY ACTION PLAN
Portland Facility, 4410 NW Front Avenue, Portland, Oregon 97210
Revised February 2021
1. Purpose and scope
This Emergency Action Plan describes what employees of Cascade Specialty Chemicals do when there is
a fire, chemical release, medical emergency, earthquake or other emergency at the Portland facility. It
applies to all 42 employees at the Portland facility, including warehouse, drivers, laboratory and office
staff, and to contractors and visitors while on site. The plan is kept in the front office and in the warehouse
break room, and a copy is available to any employee on request.
2. Alarm system
The building has a monitored fire alarm system with audible horns and strobe lights in the warehouse,
laboratory, loading dock and offices. The alarm is monitored 24 hours a day by Cascade Fire & Safety
under a service contract. Manual pull stations are located at each exit door. The alarm is tested on the first
Monday of each month by the facilities lead. A continuous horn means evacuate. Three short horns
repeated means shelter in place because of an outdoor hazard.
3. Evacuation procedures
When the continuous alarm sounds, all employees stop work, secure nothing that requires more than a
few seconds, and leave by the nearest marked exit. Exit routes are posted on the evacuation maps at each
exit door and in Appendix A. Warehouse staff leave by the east dock doors or the north pedestrian door.
Laboratory staff leave by the laboratory's own exterior door on the south wall. Office staff leave by the
main entrance or the west stairwell. Do not use the freight lift. Do not return for belongings.
The assembly point is the far north end of the visitor parking lot, beside the flagpole, at least 150 feet
from the building. Employees assigned as floor wardens (one per area, listed on the warden roster posted
beside each evacuation map) sweep their area, close doors behind them, and report to the assembly point.
For a chemical release outdoors or a hazard that makes leaving the building unsafe, the shelter-in-place
signal sounds. Employees move to the interior conference room or the laboratory corridor, close doors,
and the facilities lead shuts down the building ventilation from the mechanical room panel.
4. Accounting for employees after evacuation
At the assembly point each floor warden takes a headcount of the people from their area against the daily
sign-in sheet and the visitor log, which the receptionist brings out. Any person unaccounted for is reported
at once to the incident coordinator at the assembly point, who passes the information to the fire
department on arrival. No one re-enters the building until the fire department or the incident coordinator
gives the all-clear. Evacuation drills are held twice a year, in spring and autumn.
5. Rescue and medical duties
Employees do not attempt rescue inside the building. First aid is given at the assembly point by the
trained first-aid responders (two per shift, named on the warden roster), who bring the first-aid kit and the
AED from the front office. An employee exposed to a chemical is taken to the emergency shower and
eyewash at the loading dock if it can be reached safely, or to the assembly point, and the SDS for the
product is brought to the responders. Emergency medical services are called for any injury beyond minor
first aid.
6. Training and review
Every new employee is walked through this plan, the exit routes for their work area and the assembly
point on their first day. Floor wardens and first-aid responders are trained annually. The plan is reviewed
with all employees whenever it is changed and whenever an employee's responsibilities under it change.
The facilities lead reviews the plan every January and updates the evacuation maps whenever the building
layout changes.
Appendix A: Evacuation maps (warehouse, laboratory, offices)
Appendix B: Floor warden and first-aid responder roster (posted beside each evacuation map)
